verdicts.why: A golf or race course is a plain name for a laid-out ground; the word takes no side on it.
A line of orientation or direction is stated neutrally; 'the course of the day' in the sentences carries no attitude.
A part of a meal served at one time is a purely descriptive division; nothing is judged.
A body of students taught together is named without approval or contempt.
A layer of masonry is a technical term with no attitude attached.
Having a strong healthy body is the meaning itself, as with 'strong' or 'fit'; the word adds no admiration or scorn beyond stating the condition.
'The people' as the common populace is a plain collective; it is 'the masses' or 'the rabble' that would judge them, not this word.
The country or town where one lives is named by relation to the speaker, like 'sister'; the belonging is the meaning, not a judgement on the place.
A household as a social unit is described neutrally; 'a broken home' or 'a good home' get their judgement from the modifier, not from 'home'.
'The home of jazz' states origin; any warmth is in the fact of flourishing that the gloss names, not an attitude the word adds.
A base station from which missions start and end is a plain operational term.
Home plate in baseball is a technical name for a fixed object; nothing is judged.
A commercial enterprise and its people is a neutral label; 'racket' or 'outfit' would carry the attitude, 'business' does not.
One's principal money-earning activity is named as plainly as 'occupation' or 'line of work'.
The volume of commercial activity ('business is slow') is a measure, not an opinion.
Business concerns collectively ('business and government') is a neutral sector name.
Customers collectively ('we lost their business') is a plain trade term with no attitude toward the customers.
Stage business is a technical theatre term for an actor's incidental action; it takes no side.
'The heart of the city' names a central area; no attitude toward that area is expressed.
A feeling of liking is a pleasant referent, but the word names the feeling without judging the person who has it or its object.
Courage to carry on ('take heart') is admirable by its meaning, as 'courage' itself is; the word adds no attitude beyond that meaning.
An inclination of a certain kind ('a kind heart', 'a hard heart') is judged by the modifier, while 'heart' itself is neutral.
The conventional heart shape is a plain figure name with no attitude.
A playing card of the hearts suit is a plain technical term.
Heart as a variety meat names a cut without approval or disgust; 'offal' would carry the attitude, this does not.
